title: 沈黙の春 ― レイチェル・カーソンと自然の声
style: 画風01・光彩のある劇場アニメ背景を基調にした歴史科学ドキュメンタリー
research_basis: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service: Rachel Carson (1907-1964), Author of the Modern Environmental Movement
U.S. EPA: Rachel Carson and Silent Spring
U.S. EPA: DDT Regulatory History and the 1972 cancellation order
Smithsonian National Museum of American History: Silent Spring, Rachel Carson, 1962
timeline: 1940s-1950s: DDT and other persistent pesticides are widely used in agriculture, forestry and mosquito control
1962: Silent Spring is published after years of research
1962-1963: the book creates public concern and strong chemical-industry criticism; federal scientific review substantially supports Carson's concerns
1963: Carson testifies before a U.S. Senate subcommittee; do not depict this as the final ban itself
1964: Carson dies; she must not appear in 1970s scenes
1972: EPA cancels nearly all remaining federal DDT registrations, with limited public-health, quarantine and export exceptions

visual_anchors.carson: Rachel Carson at about age 55: short softly waved brown-gray hair, oval face, plain mid-century blouse and dark tailored jacket, restrained expression; a scientist-writer, never a glamorous celebrity
visual_anchors.student: the same modern 17-year-old Japanese male student used in H040-H042, short black hair, navy school coat, gray scarf and black backpack
visual_anchors.book: a modest 1962 hardcover represented without readable generated title; use its physical form, bird silhouette and green-blue cloth only

science_accuracy: show persistence and biomagnification through field sampling, water, fish, birds of prey and fragile eggs rather than glowing poison or fantasy arrows
do not claim every pesticide has identical effects or that all insects must be eliminated
Carson did not demand abandonment of all chemical pest control; her argument concerned indiscriminate use and persistent chemicals such as DDT
the silent spring is a warning and imagined consequence, not footage of a literal nationwide birdless spring
human risk is represented through careful medical and tissue sampling, not sensational mass casualties
bird population harm can be shown through DDE-associated eggshell thinning and reproductive failure, not instant adult-bird death
history_accuracy: chemical-industry attacks are professional and rhetorical: hostile reviews, press conferences and legal pressure, never physical violence
Carson's public influence is collective: readers, scientists, journalists, civic groups, congressional review and later regulators all contribute
do not place an EPA logo or agency scene before 1970
separate the 1962 publication, 1963 Senate testimony and 1972 EPA decision visually
do not show Carson witnessing or signing the 1972 order because she died in 1964
show the modern environmental movement as a broad civic and scientific development, not a single-person victory

composition.subtitle_safe_area: keep faces, hands, book, samples, birds, nests and official actions above the lower 45 percent
composition.camera: one stable push, pull or hold per shot
composition.text: no readable generated book titles, articles, hearing placards, chemical labels, orders, posters or signs

avoid: photorealism, oil-paint texture, disaster-movie imagery or fantasy green poison
a single spray instantly killing all wildlife
Carson appearing in 1970s EPA or Earth Day scenes
claiming a complete worldwide DDT ban in 1972
modern laboratory screens or contemporary protective equipment in 1950s-1960s scenes
readable generated text, logos, watermarks or fake quotations
